Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 45, verses 3–5:

Allah's statement ﴿Indeed, in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning in their creation, ﴿are signs for the believers﴾. ﴿And in your creation and what He disperses of creatures are signs for a people who are certain﴾. ﴿And in the alternation of night and day, and what Allah sends down from the sky of provision﴾, meaning the rain, ﴿by which He revives the earth after its death, and in the turning of the winds are signs for a people who reason﴾. All of this has been discussed fully in al-Baqarah and elsewhere [[See vol. 2, p. 191 and following, and vol. 14, p. (58)]].

The common reading is ﴿wa-ma yabuththu min dabbah ayatun﴾ and ﴿wa-tasrifi al-riyahi ayatun﴾, with the final word in the nominative (raf') in both. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read both with a kasra on the taa' (ayatin). There is no disagreement about the first, that it is in the accusative as the noun of inna (ism inna) with its predicate ﴿fi al-samawati﴾.

The reasoning for the kasra in the second ayat is that it is coordinated (ataf) with what inna governs, the implied sense being: "And indeed in your creation and what He disperses of creatures are signs." As for the third, it is said that the accusative there is a repetition of ayat because the sentence has grown long, as you say: "I struck Zayd, Zayd" [[In manuscript L: "Zaydan wa-Zayd", with a waw added.]]. It is also said that it is governed by what inna governs, on the assumption that fi is omitted, the sense being: "And in the alternation of night and day are signs." So fi was dropped because it had already been mentioned. Sibawayh cited for this ellipsis the verse:

"Is every man you think a man... and a fire kindling at night?"

Here he omitted "kulla" (every), which was in construct with "nar" (fire), which is in the genitive, because it had been mentioned earlier.

It is also said that this is a case of coordinating over two governing elements (al-'atf 'ala 'amilayn, coordination upon two operators). Sibawayh did not permit this, but al-Akhfash and a group of the Kufans did. Thus "ikhtilaf" (alternation) is coordinated on "wa-fi khalqikum" and then he says "wa-tasrifi al-riyahi ayatun," which requires coordination over two governing elements. Coordination over two governing elements is considered faulty, because coordinating particles stand in the place of the governor, so they cannot stand in for two differing governors. If it stood in for a nominative governor and an accusative governor at once, it would be both nominative and accusative in one position.

As for the reading with the nominative, it is taken as a reference to the position (mawdi') of inna together with what it governs. The grammarians also required coordination over two governing elements here, since it is coordinated on "wa-ikhtilafi" (in "wa-fi khalqikum"), and "ayatun" is coordinated on the position of the first "ayatun", but this is understood as the repetition of fi. It is also permissible to read it in the nominative as an inceptive (qat') separate from what precedes it, so it is nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and what precedes it is its predicate, making it coordination of one sentence on another. Al-Farra' transmitted the nominative for both "ikhtilaf" and "ayatun", and made "ikhtilaf" itself the signs.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These are the signs of Allah﴾, meaning: these are the signs of Allah, that is, His proofs and evidences that point to His oneness and His power. "We recite them to you in truth", meaning with the truth that contains no falsehood and no lie. It is also read "yatluhā" with the ya' (third person). So in what speech after Allah [[The text between the two brackets is an addition from manuscripts L and N.]] "It was said: after His Qur'an", and His signs, will they believe? The reading of the majority is with the ya' (yu'minūn), as a report. Ibn Muhaysin, and Abu Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read "tu'minūn" with the ta' (second person), as address.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verses 7–8:**

Allah's words: ﴿Woe to every sinful liar﴾. "Wayl" (woe) is a valley in Hell. He threatens those who abandon reflection upon His signs. "Al-affak" is the liar, the one who lies much, and "al-ifk" is falsehood.

"Athim" means one who commits sin (ithm). It is said that the intended person is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, according to what he narrated. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that he was al-Harith ibn Kaladah. Al-Tha'labi related that he was Abu Jahl and his companions.

"Who hears the signs of Allah recited to him" means the verses of the Qur'an. "Then persists, arrogant" means he persists in his disbelief, magnifying himself in his own soul so as not to submit. It is derived from "sarra al-surrata" (he tied the bag), when he tied it shut. Ibn Abbas and others said this is its meaning. It was also said that its origin is from "israr al-himar 'ala al-'anah" (the donkey's persistence over the she-ass), which is when he bends over her with his ears laid back. [[Al-'anah: the she-ass (the female donkey).]]

The "an" in "ka'anna" is the lightened form of the heavy "anna", as if he did not hear it, and its pronoun is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), as in the verse:

"As if a gazelle were grazing toward the green acacia tree" [[It is also narrated as "toward the tender acacia tree" (wari' al-salm). This is the second half of a verse by Ibn Suraym al-Yashkuri, whose first half, as it appears in the Kitab of Sibawayh and al-Maqasid al-Nahwiyyah, is:

"And one day she met us with a noble face."

Al-muqsam: the beautiful. "Ta'tu": to reach out and take. "Al-salm": a specific tree. He described a woman of beautiful face and compared her to a gazelle with abundant pasture.]]

The clause's position is in the accusative (nasb), meaning: he persists like one who did not hear. The meaning of this verse was discussed earlier at the beginning of "Luqman" [[See vol. 14, p. (57).]]. The meaning of "So give them good tidings of a painful punishment" was discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, pp. 198 and 238, second or third printing.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 9–10:

Allah's saying: ﴿And when he learns anything of Our revelations, he takes it in mockery﴾. This is like his saying about the zaqqum (a tree in Hell): "It is butter and dates," and his saying about the guardians of Hell: "If they are nineteen, I alone will deal with them." ﴿For those there is a humiliating punishment﴾: degrading and disgracing. ﴿Before them is Hell﴾: that is, behind what they are in of pride in the world and their arrogance towards the truth, there is Hell. Ibn 'Abbas said: "﴿Before them is Hell﴾" means "in front of them," like His saying ﴿Before him is Hell, and he will be given to drink of pus-like water﴾ [Ibrahim: 16], meaning in front of him. He (the poet) said:

"Is it not before me, if my death is delayed, that I crawl with the boys, creeping like the eagle?"

﴿Neither will what they earned avail them at all﴾: that is, of wealth and children. Its like is His saying ﴿Neither their wealth nor their children will avail them against Allah at all﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 10], meaning of wealth and children. ﴿Nor those they took as protectors besides Allah﴾: meaning the idols. ﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾: that is, lasting and painful.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 45, verse 11:**

His statement, may He be exalted, ﴿This is guidance﴾ is a mubtada' (grammatical subject, نَ "al-mubtada'") and khabar (predicate, "al-khabar"), meaning the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means everything that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. ﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of their Lord﴾ means they denied its proofs.

﴿For them is a punishment of a painful rijz﴾. Al-rijz (a torment, "al-rijz") means punishment. That is, for them is a punishment of a painful punishment. Its evidence is His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a plague from the sky﴾[[Verse 59 of Surah al-Baqarah.]] [al-Baqarah: 59], meaning a punishment.

It was also said that al-rijz means filth, like al-rijs, and this is like His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿and he will be given to drink of pus-like water﴾[[Verse 16 of Surah Ibrahim.]] [Ibrahim: 16], meaning that for them is a punishment from having to swallow a filthy drink.

Ibn Muhaysin read the راء (ra') of al-rijz with a damma wherever it occurs. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin and Hafs read ﴿painful﴾ (ألِيمٌ, "alim") in the nominative (with raf'), according to the meaning: for them is a painful punishment (عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ, "adhab alim") from rijz. The rest read it in the genitive (with khafd) as an adjective (na't) of al-rijz.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 12–13:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is Allah who subjected the sea to you, that the ships may sail upon it by His command, and that you may seek of His bounty, and that you may be thankful.﴾ He mentioned the completeness of His power and the perfection of His blessing upon His servants, and He made clear that He created what He created for their benefits. "And He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, all of it from Him." That is, this is His action, His creation, and His kindness and favour.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Jahdari and others read "jami'an minhu" with a kasra on the mim, a shaddah on the nun and tanwin on the ha', in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). Abu 'Amr said: And thus I heard Maslamah recite it as "minnatan," meaning by way of bounty and generosity. And also from Maslamah ibn Muharib: "jami'an mannuhu," with mann attached to the pronominal ha' (of possession). According to Abu Hatim, it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: that is, or it is from Him. The recitation of the majority is manifest.

﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿Tell those who believe to forgive﴾ is in the jussive mood because it answers the command "tell" (qul), by analogy with the conditional and its response, as in your saying: "Stand up and you will get some good."

It was also said that it is jussive by the deletion of the lam (of command). And it was said that the meaning is: "Tell them, 'Forgive,' and they will forgive," so that it is a response to a deleted command that the context indicates. This was said by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa, and Ibn al-ʿArabi preferred it.

The verse was revealed because a man from Quraysh insulted ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, and ʿUmar intended to lash out at him. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "This is not authentic."

Al-Wahidi, al-Qushayri and others mention, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, that the verse was revealed concerning ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy during the expedition against Banu al-Mustaliq. They had camped by a well called "al-Muraysi'," and ʿAbd Allah sent his slave boy to draw water. He was slow, so ʿAbd Allah said, "What delayed you?" He replied, "The slave of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab sat at the mouth of the well, and he did not leave anyone to draw water until he had filled the waterskins of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the waterskins of Abu Bakr, and he filled them for his master." ʿAbd Allah said, "Our case and theirs is only like what is said: 'Fatten your dog and it will eat you.'" This reached ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, so he wrapped himself in his sword, intending to go to him and kill him, and Allah revealed this verse. This is the narration of ʿAta' from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Maymun ibn Mihran also narrated from him, saying: When ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245] was revealed, a Jew in Medina called Finhas said: "The Lord of Muhammad has become poor!" He said: When ʿUmar heard of this, he wrapped himself in his sword and went out in pursuit of him. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Your Lord says to you: 'Tell those who believe to forgive those who do not hope for the Days of Allah.'"[[Verse 245 of Surat al-Baqarah.]]

Know that ʿUmar had wrapped himself in his sword and gone out in pursuit of the Jew. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent someone after him, and when he came, he said: "O ʿUmar, put down your sword." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, you have spoken the truth. I testify that you were sent with the truth." He said: "Indeed your Lord says: 'Tell those who believe to forgive those who do not hope for the Days of Allah.'" He said: "La jaram (indeed, certainly)! By the One who sent you with the truth, you will not see anger in my face."

I say: What al-Mahdawi and al-Nahhas mention is the narration of al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it is the view of al-Qurazi and al-Suddi. On this view, the abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation) applies to the verse. But if the verse was revealed in Medina or during the expedition against Banu al-Mustaliq, then it is not abrogated.

The meaning of "yaghfiru" is: they pardon and overlook. The meaning of "lā yarjūna ayyāma Allāh" is: they do not hope for His reward. It was also said: they do not fear the might and punishment of Allah. It was also said: "rajāʾ" here means "khawf" (fear), as in His saying: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not expect dignity from Allah?﴾ [Nuh: 13], meaning: you do not fear His greatness. The meaning is: you do not fear a punishment like that of the earlier nations. "Days" is used to refer to events. It was also said: they do not hope for Allah's victory for His allies and His striking of His enemies. It was also said: the meaning is they do not fear the Resurrection.

"Liyajziya qawman bima kanu yaksibun" (that He may recompense a people for what they used to earn): the common reading is "liyajziya" with the yāʾ, meaning "that Allah may recompense." Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Ibn ʿĀmir read "linajziya" with the nūn, as an expression of majesty. Abu Jaʿfar, al-Aʿraj and Shayba read "liyujzā" with a yāʾ that is vowelled with a ḍamma and a zāy with a fatḥa, as a passive verb, and "qawman" in the accusative. Abu ʿAmr said: "This is a clear grammatical error (laḥn)." Al-Kisāʾī said: its meaning is "that the recompense may recompense a people," and its parallel is "Thus We rescue the believers," in the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir and Abu Bakr in Surat al-Anbiya' [see vol. 11, p. 334].

The poet said:

"Even if Qufayra had borne the pup of a dog,
the pup would have made all the dogs be cursed."

The poet, Jarir, is satirizing al-Farazdaq. Qufayra (on the pattern of Juhayna) is the mother of al-Farazdaq.

That is, "the pup would have been cursed with the curse."
Already mentioned [[see vol. 15, p. 370.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verses 16–17:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We indeed gave the Children of Israel the Book﴾, meaning the Torah. "And the judgment and prophethood." Al-hukm: understanding of the Book. It is also said: al-hukm is judging among people and adjudication. "And prophethood," meaning the prophets from the time of Yusuf (peace be upon him) until the time of Isa (peace be upon him). "And We provided them with good things" (al-tayyibat), i.e., what is lawful of foods, fruits and provisions, which were in al-Sham. It is also said: it means the manna and quails in the wilderness (al-tih). "And We preferred them over the worlds," i.e., over the worlds of their time, as explained earlier in "al-Dukhan" [[see vol. 16, p.]]. "And We gave them clear proofs concerning the matter." Ibn Abbas said: it means the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the signs of his prophethood, that he would migrate from Tihama to Yathrib, and the people of Yathrib would support him. It is also said: the clear proofs of the matter are plain laws concerning the lawful and the unlawful, and miracles. "Then they did not differ except after knowledge had come to them," meaning Yusha' ibn Nun; some of them believed and some disbelieved, related by al-Naqqash. It is also said: "except after knowledge had come to them" refers to the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), and they differed concerning it. "Out of envy among themselves," i.e., jealousy of the Prophet (ﷺ), as al-Dahhak said. It is also said: the meaning of "baghyan" is that some of them transgressed against others, seeking superiority and leadership, and they killed the prophets. Likewise the polytheists of your era, O Muhammad, the clear proofs have come to them, but they turned away from them out of rivalry for leadership. "Indeed your Lord will judge between them," i.e., will decide and separate. "On the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ" in the worldly life.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 18:

There are two issues here.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then We put you on a [clear] way of the affair﴾. The shari'ah (the way, the path laid down) in language means the course of action and the religion (millah). It is also said of the watering place of the water, which is the place where drinkers come to drink: shari'ah. From this comes "al-shari'" (the main road), because it is a path to the destination. So the shari'ah is what Allah has prescribed for His servants of the religion, and its plural is shara'i'. The shara'i' in religion are the paths (madhahib) which Allah has prescribed for His creation. So the meaning of "We put you on a way of the affair" is: on a clear method of the matter of religion, which leads you to the truth.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "on a shari'ah" means on guidance from the affair. Qatadah said: the shari'ah is the command, the prohibition, the limits and the obligations. Muqatil said: the clear proof, because it is a path to the truth. Al-Kalbi said: the sunnah, because he follows the way of those prophets who came before him. Ibn Zayd said: the religion, because it is the path of salvation.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: The word "amr" occurs in language with two meanings. One of them is the meaning of "matter/affair (sha'n)", as in His saying: ﴿So they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ [[Qur'an 11:97.]] [Hud: 97]. The second is one of the two categories of speech, the opposite of which is the prohibition (nahy). Both may be intended here. Its implied meaning: "Then We placed you on a way of the religion, which is the millah of Islam," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then We revealed to you: Follow the millah of Ibrahim, a hanif, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [[Qur'an 16:123.]] [al-Nahl: 123]. There is no disagreement that Allah, exalted is He, did not differ among the shara'i' regarding monotheism, noble conduct and the public good, but He differed between them in the subsidiary rulings (furu'), as He, glorified is He, knew.

The second issue: Ibn al-'Arabi said: Some of those who speak on knowledge (religious sciences) thought that this verse is evidence that the shari'ah of those before us is not a shari'ah for us, because Allah, exalted is He, singled out the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community in this verse with a shari'ah. We do not deny that the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community are distinguished by a shari'ah; the disagreement concerns what the Prophet (ﷺ) reported of the shari'ah of those before us in the context of praise and commendation, whether following it is obligatory or not.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not follow the desires of those who do not know﴾, meaning the polytheists. Ibn 'Abbas said: Qurayzah and al-Nadir. And from him: it was revealed when Quraysh invited him to the religion of his forefathers.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they will never avail you against Allah at all﴾, meaning: if you follow their desires, they will not repel from you any of the punishment of Allah at all. "And indeed, the wrongdoers are allies of one another," meaning: friends, helpers, and loved ones. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means that the hypocrites are allies of the Jews. "And Allah is the Ally of the righteous," meaning: their helper and supporter. And "the righteous" here are those who guard against shirk (polytheism) and sins.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is insights for mankind﴾. It is an inchoative (mubtada') and a predicate (khabar). That is, "This which I have sent down to you is proofs, indications, and signposts for people concerning the prescribed limits and the rulings." It is also recited as "هذه بصائر" (hadhihi basa'ir), meaning: these are the verses.

﴿And guidance﴾: that is, right direction and a path that leads to Paradise for whoever adheres to it. ﴿And mercy﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿for a people who have certainty﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will treat them like those who believe and do righteous deeds?﴾ That is, those who acquired them. Al-ijtirah (acquisition, earning) means acquiring, and from it comes al-jawarih (the limbs, the instruments of acquisition), which was discussed earlier in Surat al-Ma'ida [see vol. 6, p. (66)].

Al-Kalbi said: "Those who committed (ijtarahu)" refers to Utba and Shayba, the sons of Rabi'a, and al-Walid ibn Utba. "Like those who believed" refers to Ali, Hamza and Ubayda ibn al-Harith, may Allah be pleased with them, when they came out against them on the Day of Badr and killed them. It was also said: it was revealed concerning a group of polytheists who said: "They will be given in the Hereafter better than what the believer is given," as the Lord reported about them in His saying: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, surely I will have the best with Him﴾ [Fussilat: 50]. [Note: this is verse 50 of Surat Fussilat.] And His saying "Or do they think" is an interrogative in the form of a coordinating question, meaning denial. Scholars of Arabic grammar permit this without coordination when it occurs in the middle of an address. Some people say there is an ellipsis in it, meaning: "And Allah is the Protector of the righteous. Do the polytheists know that, or do they think that We make them equal?" It was also said: it is the disjunctive "am," and the meaning of the hamza in it is the denial of such supposition.

The common reading is "sawa'" with a nominative ending, as the predicate of a fronted subject, meaning: their living and their dying are equal. The pronoun in "mahyahum wa mamatuhum" refers to the disbelievers, meaning: their living is the living of evil, and their dying is likewise.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash read "sawa'" with a accusative ending, and Abu Ubayd preferred it, saying: its meaning is "We make them equal." Al-A'mash and also Isa ibn Umar read "wa mamatahum" with an accusative ending, meaning "equal in their living and their dying"; when the preposition was dropped, it took the accusative. It is also permissible that "mahyahum wa mamatuhum" be a substitute (badal) for the hā' and mīm in "najalahum," the meaning being: that We make their living and their dying equal to the living and dying of those who believe. It is also permissible that the pronoun in "mahyahum wa mamatuhum" refers to the disbelievers and the believers together. Mujahid said: the believer dies a believer and is resurrected a believer, and the disbeliever dies a disbeliever and is resurrected a disbeliever.

Ibn al-Mubarak reported to us: Shu'ba reported to us from Amr ibn Murra, from Abu al-Duha, from Masruq, who said: A man from the people of Makkah said: "This was the station of Tamim al-Dari. I saw him one night until morning, or nearly until morning, reciting a verse from the Book of Allah, bowing, prostrating and weeping: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will treat them like those who believe and do righteous deeds?﴾" to the end of the whole verse.

Bashir said: I spent a night with al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym. He stood to pray, and passed by this verse, and he remained through the night until morning, repeating nothing but it, with intense weeping. Ibrahim ibn al-Ash'ath said: I often saw al-Fudayl ibn Iyad repeating this verse and its like from the beginning of the night to its end, then he would say: "I wish I knew: to which of the two groups do you belong?" This verse was called "the weeping place of the worshippers" (mabkat al-'abidin), because it is muhkam (clear, unabrogated in meaning).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾, i.e., with the true command. "And that every soul may be recompensed," i.e., so that it may be recompensed. "For what it has earned," i.e., in the Hereafter. "And they will not be wronged."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 23:

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "That disbeliever has taken his desire (hawa) as his religion, so he does not desire anything without mounting it." 'Ikrimah said: "Have you seen one who makes his god, whom he worships, what he desires or finds pleasing? When he finds something pleasing and desires it, he takes it as a god." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "One of them would worship a stone, and when he saw something better than it, he would cast it away and worship the other." Muqatil said: "It was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi, one of the mockers, because he used to worship whatever his soul desired." Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: "They worshipped stones only because the House (the Ka'bah) is made of stone." It has also been said: "The meaning is: Have you seen one who submits to his desire and to what he worships? (This is) a marvel to people of intellect at this ignorance." Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: "In this verse there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir); its meaning is: Have you seen one who has taken his desire as his god?" Al-Sha'bi said: "Desire (al-hawa) was only so named because it plunges (yahwi) its companion into the Fire." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah has not mentioned hawa in the Qur'an except to condemn it. Allah the Exalted said: 'And he followed his desire, so his likeness is like the likeness of the dog'" [al-A'raf: 176]. And the Exalted said: ﴿And he follows his desire, and his affair is ever in excess﴾ [al-Kahf: 28]. And the Exalted said: "Rather, those who wronged followed their desires without knowledge. So who can guide one whom Allah has sent astray?" [al-Rum: 29]. And the Exalted said: ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ [al-Qasas: 50]. And the Exalted said: ﴿And do not follow desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾ [Sad: 26].

Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "None of you truly believes until his desire is subject to what I have brought." Abu Umamah said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'No god worshipped under the heavens is more hateful to Allah than desire.'" Shaddad ibn Aws reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The shrewd one is he who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death. The foolish one is he who follows his soul's desires and wishes (vainly) for things from Allah." The Prophet, peace be upon him, also said: "When you see avarice obeyed, desire followed, the world preferred, and every man pleased with his own opinion, then keep to yourself and leave the affairs of the common people." He (ﷺ) also said: "Three things destroy and three things save. The destroyers are obeyed avarice, followed desire, and a man's self-admiration. The saviours are fear of Allah in private and in public, moderation in wealth and poverty, and justice in contentment and anger." Abu al-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "When a man rises in the morning, his desire, his deed and his knowledge are gathered together. If his deed follows his desire, his day is a day of evil; if his deed follows his knowledge, his day is a good day."

Al-Asma'i said: "I heard a man say:

Humiliation (hawan) is desire (hawa) with its name inverted,
So when you desire, you have met humiliation."

Ibn al-Muqaffa' was asked about hawa and said: "It is hawan (humiliation) whose nun was stolen." Then a poet took it and versified:

The nun of humiliation has been stolen from desire,
So when you desire, you have met humiliation.

Another said:

Indeed desire is humiliation itself,
So when you desire, you have earned humiliation.
And when you desire, desire has enslaved you,
So submit to your love, whoever he may be.

'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said:

Among afflictions is a sign of affliction:
That no turning away from your desire is seen in you.
The slave is the slave of the soul in its appetites,
While the free man sometimes eats and sometimes hungers.

Ibn Duraid said:

When the soul one day demands from you a desire,
And there is a way to oppose it,
Then leave it and oppose what it desires, for your desire is an enemy,
And opposition is a friend.

Abu 'Ubayd al-Tusi said:

And if you give the soul its wish,
It opens its mouth wide toward its desire.

Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawari said: "I passed by a monk and found him emaciated, so I said to him: 'You are ill.' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'Since when?' He said: 'Since I came to know myself.' I said: 'Do you not seek treatment?' He said: 'Medicine has defeated me, and I have resolved on cauterization.' I said: 'And what is cauterization?' He said: 'Opposing desire.'" Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah al-Tustari said: "Your desire is your disease; if you oppose it, it is your cure." Wahb said: "If you are in doubt between two matters and do not know which is better, look at the one farther from your desire and go to it."

For the scholars there are books and chapters on this subject, condemning desire and opposing it, and we have pointed to what is sufficient from it. Enough for you is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿But as for he who feared the station of his Lord and restrained the soul from desire, indeed, Paradise will be his refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 40-41].

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And Allah sent him astray knowingly﴾, i.e., with knowledge that He already had of him. It has been said: He sent him astray from reward with knowledge from Him that he did not deserve it. Ibn 'Abbas said: "That is, with knowledge that had already preceded with Him that he would go astray." Muqatil said: "With knowledge from Him that he is misguided; the meanings are close." It has also been said: "With knowledge, on the part of the idol-worshipper, that it neither benefits nor harms." Then it was said: "'With knowledge' may be a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject (the doer): the meaning is: He sent him astray while He had knowledge of him, i.e., He sent him astray knowing that he is among the people of misguidance in His prior knowledge." It may also be a circumstantial clause referring to the object, so the meaning is: He sent him astray in a state in which the disbeliever knew that he was astray.

"And sealed upon his hearing and his heart": i.e., He set a seal upon his hearing so that he does not hear admonition, and sealed his heart so that he does not understand guidance. "And placed upon his sight a covering": i.e., a veil, so that he does not see right guidance. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "ghashwah" with a fatha on the ghayn and without an alif, and this has been discussed in al-Baqarah (see vol. 1, p. 191 of the second or third printed edition). The poet said:

By Him whom I serve, and by your right hand,
I swear, and you hold up your oath:
If you have clothed me in a covering,
Indeed I had purified my love for you for a time.

"Then who can guide him after Allah?": i.e., after He has sent him astray. "Will you not then remember?": that you may take heed and know that He is capable of whatever He wills. This verse refutes the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine decree) and the Imamiyyah and whoever follows their path in belief, since it plainly states that they are prevented from guidance. Then it has been said: "And sealed upon his hearing and his heart" is said in the form of a report about their conditions. It has also been said that it is in the form of an invocation against them, as has been mentioned at the beginning of al-Baqarah (see vol. 1, p. 186).

Ibn Jurayj related that it was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Qays from the Ghayatilah (the clan of Banu Qays ibn 'Adi, whom Ibn Duraid in his book al-Ishtiqaq (p. 75, European edition) describes as men of Quraysh called "al-Ghayatil," with Qays being the chief of Quraysh in his time, unchallenged; he said: "al-Ghayatil is the plural of ghaytalah, meaning dense trees and the mingling of darkness"). Al-Naqqash related that it was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, because he once circumambulated the House one night with al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and they talked about the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Jahl said: "By Allah, I know that he is truthful!" Al-Walid said to him: "Be quiet! What makes you know that?" He said: "O Abu 'Abd Shams, in his youth we used to call him 'the truthful, the trustworthy,' but when his intellect matured and his judgment was perfected, we call him 'the liar, the traitor!' By Allah, I know that he is truthful!" He said: "Then what prevents you from believing him and believing in him?" He said: "The daughters of Quraysh will talk about me, that I followed the orphan of Abu Talib for the sake of a morsel (kisrah) [in one manuscript: kusayrah]. By al-Lat and al-'Uzza, I will never follow him!" So it was revealed: "And sealed upon his hearing and his heart."

**Al-Qurtubi's Commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 45, Verse 24**

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿They say, "There is nothing but our worldly life. We die and we live."﴾ This is a denial by them of the Hereafter, a rejection of resurrection, and a negation of recompense.

The meaning of "we die and we live" is: we die and our children live. This is related from al-Kalbi. It is also read as "wa-nahya" with a ḍamma on the nūn. It is said: some of us die and some of us live. It is also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in it, meaning "we live and we die," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud.

"And nothing destroys us except time (al-dahr)." Mujahid said: it means the years and the days. Qatadah said: "except the lifespan," and the meaning is one. It is read "except a passing time (dahrun yamurru)." Ibn 'Uyaynah said: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to say, "Time is what destroys us, and it is what gives us life and causes us to die." So this verse was revealed. Qutrub said: "And nothing destroys us except death," and he recited the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Do you grieve because of the fates and their vicissitudes...
while time does not blame the one who despairs."

Ikrimah said: that is, "and nothing destroys us except Allah."

Abu Hurayrah related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The people of the Jahiliyyah used to say, 'Nothing destroys us except the night and the day,' and it is they that destroy us, cause us to die, and give us life." So they revile time. Allah the Exalted says: "The son of Adam hurts Me; he reviles time, but I am Time. In My hand is the affair; I alternate the night and the day." I say: His words "Allah said" to the end are the text of al-Bukhari and its wording. Muslim and Abu Dawud also narrated it. In the Muwatta', from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Let none of you say, 'O misfortune of time (ya khaybata al-dahr),' for Allah is Time (al-dahr)."

Those who hold that "al-Dahr" is one of the names of Allah have used this hadith as evidence. Whoever does not regard it as a name said that it came as a rebuttal of the Arabs in their Jahiliyyah, for they used to believe that time is the agent, as Allah reported about them in this verse. So whenever harm, injustice, or something disliked befell them, they attributed it to time. It was said to them concerning that: "Do not revile time, for Allah is Time," meaning: Allah is the agent of these matters which you attribute to time, so the reviling returns to Him, glorified is He, and they were forbidden from that. What confirms the soundness of this is the hadith of Abu Hurayrah which we have mentioned: he said, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, says: The son of Adam hurts Me..." and the hadith continues.

And well did the one say it, Abu 'Ali al-Thaqafi:

"O you who blame time when it befalls him,
do not blame time for its treachery.
Time is ordered, and it has an orderer,
and time ends at His command.
How many a disbeliever whose wealth is abundant,
which multiplies manifold despite his disbelief,
and a believer who has no dirham,
whose faith increases despite his poverty."

It is narrated that Salim ibn 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar often mentioned time, so his father rebuked him and said: "Beware, my son, of mentioning time!" And he recited:

"Time is not the one who commits a deed for its own sake,
nor the one who brings trials, so do not revile time.
But whenever Allah sends a sender
upon a people, He turns their ease into hardship."

Abu 'Ubayd said: I debated with some of the heretics (mulhidah), and he said: "Do you not see that He says, 'For Allah is Time'?" I said: Did anyone ever revile Allah throughout the ages? Rather, they used to say, as al-A'sha said:

"Whether one stays or departs,
and in the journey, when they passed, there was a pause.
Allah has monopolized faithfulness and justice,
and has turned away blame from the man."

Abu 'Ubayd said: It is characteristic of the Arabs to censure time at calamities and misfortunes, so much so that they mentioned it in their poetry and attributed events to it. 'Amr ibn Qami'ah said:

"The daughters of time have shot me from where I do not see;
how then is one shot who is not a shooter?
Had they been arrows, I would have guarded against them,
but I am shot without arrows.
Upon my two palms once, and upon the staff,
I lean, then after them three times I rise."

Similar to this there is much in poetry: they attribute that to time and ascribe it to it, while Allah, glorified is He, is the Agent, and there is no lord besides Him.

﴿And they have no knowledge of that﴾, meaning, no knowledge. The "min" here is extra (za'idah), meaning: they said it while doubting. ﴿They only conjecture﴾, meaning: they only speak by conjecture.

The polytheists were of several kinds: among them were these, and among them were those who affirmed the Creator (al-Sani') but denied resurrection, and among them were those who doubted resurrection and did not firmly deny it. Groups also arose in Islam who could not deny resurrection out of fear of the Muslims, so they interpreted it allegorically, considering the Resurrection to be the death of the body, and considering reward and punishment to be imaginings that befall the spirits, according to their claim. The evil of these people is more harmful than the evil of all the disbelievers, because these ones obscure the truth, and the apparent appearance of their obfuscation deceives people. The openly declared polytheist is one whom the Muslim guards against.

It is also said: "We die and our traces live," and this is the life of remembrance (hayat al-dhikr). It is also said that they pointed to metempsychosis (al-tanasukh, the transmigration of souls), meaning that a man dies and his soul is placed in a lifeless body (mawat) and is thereby revived.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾, meaning: and when Our verses revealed concerning the possibility of resurrection are recited to these polytheists, there is no rebuttal from them, ﴿their argument is only that they say: "Bring our fathers, if you are truthful."﴾ "Hujjatahum" (their argument) is the predicate of kana (was), and the subject is ﴿only that they say: "Bring our fathers"﴾, i.e., the dead, that we may ask them about the truth of what you say. So Allah answered them with His words: ﴿Say: "Allah gives you life"﴾, meaning, after you were lifeless drops of semen, ﴿then He causes you to die, then He will gather you to the Day of Resurrection﴾, just as He gave you life in this world. ﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾ that Allah will restore them just as He originated them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why did He call their statement an argument when it is not an argument? I say: Because they put it forward as a person making an argument puts forward his proof, and they set it in the manner of such proof; so it was called an argument by way of mockery (tahakkum). Or, because in their reckoning and assumption it is an argument. Or, because it is in the style of the saying:

*"A greeting among them is a painful blow"*[[This is the second half of a verse by ʿAmr ibn Maʿdi Karib. Its first half is:

*"And cavalry that advanced against them with cavalry."*

He means: when they meet in battle, they exchange in place of a greeting the painful blow. Dalafat means advanced; al-dalif means close-stepping in walking.]]

As if it were said: "Their argument was only that which is not an argument." The intended meaning is the negation that they have any argument at all. If you ask: how does Allah's saying ﴿Say: "Allah gives you life"﴾ serve as an answer to ﴿"Bring our fathers, if you are truthful"﴾? I say: When they denied resurrection and disbelieved the messengers, and supposed that what they said was a rebuke that silences the other, they were bound by what they themselves acknowledged, namely that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is He who gives them life and then causes them to die. To this binding He added a binding to what is obligatory to affirm, if they were fair and listened to the call of truth, namely their gathering on the Day of Resurrection. Whoever is able to do that is able to bring their fathers, and that is the easiest thing for Him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, both in creation and in ownership. "And the Day the Hour establishes, that Day the falsifiers will be lost." The first "yawm" (day) is in the accusative, governed by "yakhsaru" (will be lost), and "yawma'idhin" (that day) is a repetition for emphasis (margin note) or an apposition. It has also been said that the implied meaning is: "And to Him belongs the dominion on the Day the Hour establishes." The governing element in "yawma'idhin" is "yakhsaru," and the object of "yakhsaru" is omitted; the meaning is: they will lose their abodes in Paradise.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will see every nation kneeling﴾, meaning from the terror of that Day. The "nation" here means the people of each religion. Regarding "kneeling" (al-jathiyah) there are five interpretations.

The first: Mujahid said it means "crouching, ready to spring up" (mustawfizah). Sufyan said: "The mustawfiz is the one of whom only his two knees and the tips of his fingers touch the ground." Al-Dahhak said: "That is at the time of the reckoning."

The second: "gathered together" (mujtama'ah), said by Ibn Abbas. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "and you will see the people of every religion gathered together."

The third: "distinguished" (mutamayyizah), said by Ikrimah.

The fourth: "submissive" (khadi'ah) in the dialect of Quraysh, said by Mu'arrij.

The fifth: "sitting back on their knees" (barikah 'ala al-rukab), said by al-Hasan.

Al-judhw (jathw) means sitting on the knees. One says: jatha 'ala rukbatayhi, yajthu, wa yajthi, judhuwwan and juthiyyan, with the pattern fu'ul in both. This has already been discussed in "Maryam" [see vol. 11, p. 132]. The root of al-juthwah (the word may be read with a third vowel on the jim) is: a group of anything. Tarafah said, describing two graves:

"You see two mounds of earth over them, with solid slabs of closely laid stone."

[Al-summ: solid. Al-munaddad: that which has been placed one upon another.]

Then it was said: this is specific to the disbelievers, said by Yahya ibn Sallam. It was also said: it is general to both believer and disbeliever, awaiting the reckoning. Sufyan ibn Uyaynah related from Amr, from Abdullah ibn Babah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is as if I see you on the al-kawm [al-kawm: the elevated places], kneeling before Hell." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Salman said: "On the Day of Resurrection there is an hour that lasts ten years, in which people fall down on their knees, so much so that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) will say: 'I ask of You today only for myself.'"

﴿Every nation will be called to its record﴾. Yahya ibn Sallam said: to its reckoning. It was also said: to its book, in which was recorded for it what it had done of good and evil, said by Muqatil, and this is the meaning of Mujahid's saying. It was also said: "its book" is what the angels wrote concerning it. It was also said: its book is that which was revealed to it, so that it may see whether they acted upon what was in it. And it was said: the Book here is the Preserved Tablet.

Ya'qub al-Hadrami read "kulla ummatin" in the accusative, as a substitute (badal) for the first "kull", because in the second there is a clarification that is absent in the first: there is nothing in its kneeling that explains the state of kneeling, as there is in the second, which mentions the cause that calls them to it, namely their being summoned to their book. It was also said: it is in the accusative by the operation of a hidden "tara" (you see). The nominative is by way of the inchoative (ibtida').

﴿Today you will be recompensed for what you used to do﴾, of good or evil.

This is Our Book (﴿هَذَا كِتابُنا﴾). It has been said that these words are from the speech of Allah to them, and it has been said that they are from the speech of the angels.

"Yanṭiqu ʿalaykum bil-ḥaqq" (it speaks against you with the truth): meaning, it bears witness. This is a metaphor (istiʿārah). It is said: "nataqa al-kitābu bi-kadhā", meaning the book made such-and-such clear.

It has also been said: they read it, and the Book reminds them of what they did, so it is as if it speaks against them. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿They will say, "Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves out nothing small or great but has counted it!"﴾ [al-Kahf 18:49]. Concerning the believers, He says: "And with Us is a Book that speaks with the truth, and they will not be wronged" [al-Mu'minun 23:62]. This has already been discussed [see vol. 10, p. 418 and vol. 12, p. 134].

Grammatically, "yanṭiqu" may be in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to "al-kitāb" or to "dhā"; or it may be a second predicate (khabar thānī) for "dhā"; or "kitābunā" may be a badal (substitute) for "hādhā" with "yanṭiqu" as the predicate.

"Innā kunnā nastansikhu mā kuntum taʿmalūn" (Indeed We used to have copied what you used to do): meaning, We used to order the copying of what you used to do.

ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Indeed Allah has angels who descend every day with a [writing] thing in which they record the deeds of the children of Adam.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: Allah has entrusted purified angels who, in Ramadan, copy from Umm al-Kitāb (the Mother of the Book, the Preserved Tablet) everything that will occur of the deeds of the children of Adam. Then they compare these with the recording angels (al-ḥafaẓah) whom Allah has assigned over the servants, every Thursday. They find that what the recording angels have brought of the servants' deeds agrees with what is in their own book, which they copied from that Book, with no addition and no deficiency. Ibn ʿAbbās said: And is copying anything but from a book?

Al-Ḥasan said: "Nastansikhu mā katabathu al-ḥafaẓah ʿalā banī Ādam," because the recording angels raise the pages of deeds to the treasurers (al-khazanah).

It has also been said: the recording angels carry each day what they wrote concerning the servant. Then, when they return to their place, the good deeds and the bad deeds are copied from it, and permissible deeds (al-mubāḥāt) are not transferred to the second copy.

It has also been said: when the angels raise the deeds of the servants to Allah, He, Mighty and Majestic, orders that what carries reward and punishment be preserved in His presence, and that what carries neither reward nor punishment be dropped from the whole.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 30–31:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, their Lord will admit them into His mercy﴾, that is, Paradise. ﴿That is the clear triumph.﴾ ﴿And as for those who disbelieved: "Were not My verses recited to you? But you were arrogant and were a people of criminals."﴾ That is, it will be said to them this. It is a rhetorical question of reproach. ﴿But you were arrogant﴾ toward accepting them. ﴿And you were a people of criminals﴾, that is, polytheists who earn sins. It is said: "So-and-so is the jarimah (provider) of his family" when he is their earner. Thus the mujrim (criminal) is one who earns sins for himself. Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾[[Qur'an 68:35.]] [al-Qalam: 35]. So the mujrim is the opposite of the Muslim, and thus he is the one guilty of disbelief.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 32:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it was said, "Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, and the Hour, there is no doubt about it"﴾, meaning: the resurrection is certain to occur. Hamzah recited "wa-as-sa'ata" (and the Hour) in the accusative, as a conjunction with "wa'd" (promise). The rest of the readers recited it in the nominative, either as a new subject (ibtida', beginning of a sentence) or as a conjunction with the position of "inna wa'da Allah" (the grammatical position of the phrase after inna). It is not good to conjoin it to the pronoun in the verbal noun, because that is not emphasized, and a pronoun in the nominative is only conjoined to without emphasis in poetry. ﴿You said, "We do not know what the Hour is,"﴾ whether it is true or false. ﴿We only assume it to be a mere assumption﴾. Its estimated reading according to al-Mubarrad: "in nahnu illa nazunnu zannan" (we are not but assuming an assumption). It was also said: the estimate is "in nazunnu illa anna-kum tazunnunna zannan" (we only assume that you assume an assumption). And it was said: that is, "and you said, 'we only assume an assumption.'" ﴿And we are not certain that the Hour is coming﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the evils of what they had done will appear to them﴾, meaning: the recompense for the evils of what they had done became manifest to them. "And what they used to mock at surrounded them", meaning: it descended upon them and encompassed them. ﴿What they used to mock at﴾ refers to the punishment of Allah.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And it will be said, "Today We forget you, just as you forgot the meeting of this your Day."﴾ That is, We will leave you in the Fire, just as you left the meeting of this Day, meaning you abandoned working for it. ﴿And your refuge is the Fire﴾ — that is, your dwelling and your place of abode. ﴿And you have no helpers﴾ — no one who will help you.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 45, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because you took the signs of Allah in mockery﴾, meaning the Qur'an. "Mockery" means play. "And the worldly life deceived you", meaning it deceived you with its falsehoods and adornments, so you thought there was nothing beyond it, and that there would be no resurrection. "So today they will not be brought out of it", meaning out of the Fire. "Nor will they be allowed to make amends", meaning they will not be made to seek pleasure (i.e., be reconciled with Allah). This has already been discussed [[see vol. 10 p. 162, vol. 14 p. 49 and vol. 15 p. 353]]. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "fa-al-yawma la yakhrujuna" with a fatha on the yā' and a ḍamma on the rā', based on His saying: ﴿Every time they wish to come out of it, they will be returned to it﴾ [[verse 20 of Surah al-Sajdah.]] [al-Sajdah: 20]. The rest read it with a ḍamma on the yā' and a fatha on the rā', based on His saying: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out﴾ [[see vol. 12 p. 153.]] [Fatir: 37], and similar verses.

Qur'an 45:36–37 in al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So all praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of all the worlds﴾. Mujahid, Humayd and Ibn Muhaysin read "Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of the worlds" in the nominative in all of them, according to the meaning "He is the Lord" (huwa rabb). "And His is the majesty" (al-kibriya'), that is, the greatness, the glory, the permanence, the dominion, the power and the perfection. "In the heavens and the earth, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise." And Allah knows best.
